Pre-eclampsia is a multisystem disorder of pregnancy characterized by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation, usually with proteinuria and/or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction.

subsections.subsection_title: HOW TO REPORT A PATIENT WITH PRE-ECLAMPSIA

blocks.text: "This is a 29-year-old G2P1 at 34 weeks' gestation with hypertension and significant proteinuria, consistent with pre-eclampsia. She is currently clinically stable with no symptoms suggestive of severe disease. I would assess her maternal laboratory parameters and fetal wellbeing and institute appropriate maternal and fetal surveillance."

"This is a 32-year-old primigravida at 31 weeks' gestation with severe hypertension of 170/112 mmHg, associated with persistent headache and visual disturbance. These findings are concerning for severe pre-eclampsia. I would urgently involve senior obstetric and anaesthetic teams, stabilise the patient, treat the severe hypertension, assess for complications, administer magnesium sulfate where indicated, assess fetal wellbeing and determine the safest timing and mode of delivery."

"This patient has pre-eclampsia complicated by suspected fetal growth restriction. The fetus has an estimated weight below the expected range for gestational age, and I would assess fetal wellbeing with CTG, amniotic fluid assessment and Doppler studies, while simultaneously monitoring the mother for progression of pre-eclampsia."

blocks.text: Systolic BP ≥160 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥110 mmHg.

blocks.text: Delivery of the fetus and placenta, after appropriate maternal stabilisation when necessary.

Q7. Why is the fetus growth restricted?

blocks.text: Because abnormal placentation and maternal endothelial dysfunction cause uteroplacental insufficiency, reducing effective placental perfusion and nutrient/oxygen delivery.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. Why is urine output important?

blocks.text: Severe pre-eclampsia can cause renal dysfunction, and reduced urine output may indicate significant disease. It is also important when administering magnesium sulfate because renal impairment increases the risk of magnesium toxicity.

content_groups.group_title: Q9. Why do you check reflexes?

blocks.text: To assess neurological irritability and to monitor for magnesium toxicity during magnesium sulfate therapy.

blocks.text: Do not spend five minutes discussing proteinuria.

"This is severe hypertension in pregnancy. I would urgently repeat/confirm the measurement using appropriate technique while simultaneously initiating maternal assessment and arranging prompt antihypertensive treatment according to protocol. I would involve senior obstetric staff and assess for maternal and fetal complications."
"The patient has pre-eclampsia at 29 weeks. Will you deliver immediately?"

"Not necessarily. If the mother and fetus are stable, expectant management may be considered in an appropriate specialist setting with close maternal and fetal surveillance. However, maternal or fetal deterioration would be an indication for delivery."

items: "Summarise your management of a woman with severe pre-eclampsia."

blocks.text: "I would admit and urgently assess the mother and fetus, involve the senior obstetric and anaesthetic teams, establish IV access and monitor vital signs, urine output and fluid balance. I would urgently treat severe hypertension with an appropriate antihypertensive, assess for maternal complications with FBC, renal and liver function and coagulation studies, and assess fetal wellbeing with CTG and ultrasound as appropriate. I would administer magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis where indicated, give antenatal corticosteroids if preterm delivery is anticipated, avoid fluid overload, and determine the timing and mode of delivery based on maternal and fetal condition."
